Yea, before the sun and the signs were created, Before the stars of the heaven were made, His name was named before the Lord of Spirits. 4. He shall be a staff to the righteous whereon to stay themselves and not fall, And he shall be the light of the Gentiles, And the hope of those who are troubled of heart. 5. All who dwell on earth shall fall down and worship before him, And will praise and bless and celebrate with song the Lord of Spirits. 6. And for this reason hath he been chosen and hidden before Him, Before the creation of the world and for evermore.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Why did Jesus repeatedly call Himself 'the Son of Man' and claim pre-existence before the world was made (John 17:5, 24)? Because in 1st-century Judaism, 'that Son of Man' was a pre-existent heavenly person existing 'before the creation of the world and for evermore' (v. 3, 6), whom 'all who dwell on earth shall fall down and worship' alongside the Lord of Spirits (v. 5)!

quotes.chapter: 1 Enoch 51:3 ('The Elect One Shall Sit on My Throne')
quotes.quote: 3. And the Elect One shall in those days sit on My throne, And his mouth shall pour forth all the secrets of wisdom and counsel: For the Lord of Spirits hath given (them) to him and hath glorified him.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In Jewish theology, no mere creature or angel is permitted to sit in heaven (cf. Talmud Hagigah 15a). Yet here God ('the Lord of Spirits') declares that the Messiah ('the Elect One') sits directly upon God's own Throne ('shall in those days sit on My throne')—compare Revelation 3:21 and Matthew 25:31.

quotes.chapter: 1 Enoch 62:5–7 (The Pre-Existent Son of Man Sitting on the Throne of His Glory)
quotes.quote: 5. And one portion of them shall look on the other, And they shall be terrified, And they shall be downcast of countenance, And pain shall seize them, When they see that Son of Man Sitting on the throne of his glory. 6. And the kings and the mighty and all who possess the earth shall bless and glorify and extol him who rules over all, who was hidden. 7. For from the beginning the Son of Man was hidden, And the Most High preserved him in the presence of His might, And revealed him to the elect.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: When Jesus said in Matthew 25:31 and 19:28, 'When the Son of Man comes in His glory... then He will sit on His glorious throne,' He was quoting this exact Second Temple Jewish concept of the pre-existent Son of Man ('from the beginning the Son of Man was hidden in the presence of the Most High') sitting on the divine Throne of Glory and being glorified by all the kings of the earth.

quotes.chapter: 1 Enoch 69:26–29 ('The Sum of Judgment Was Given Unto the Son of Man')
quotes.quote: 26. And there was great joy amongst them, And they blessed and glorified and extolled Because the name of that Son of Man had been revealed unto them. 27. And he sat on the throne of his glory, And the sum of judgement was given unto the Son of Man, And he caused the sinners to pass away and be destroyed from off the face of the earth, And those who have led the world astray. 28. With chains shall they be bound, And in their assemblage-place of destruction shall they be imprisoned, And all their works vanish from the face of the earth. 29. And from henceforth there shall be nothing corruptible; For that Son of Man has appeared, And has seated himself on the throne of his glory, And all evil shall pass away before his face, And the word of that Son of Man shall go forth
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Look at verse 27 ('And he sat on the throne of his glory, And the sum of judgement was given unto the Son of Man') alongside Jesus' claim in John 5:22, 27: 'The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all will honor the Son even as they honor the Father... and He gave Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man.'

Philo of Alexandria.note: Philo Judaeus of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – AD 50) was a prominent 1st-century Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar who lived at the exact time of Jesus and died before the New Testament was written. Expounding the Hebrew Scriptures from a purely Jewish perspective, Philo proves that 1st-century Jews already believed in a Second Divine Person alongside the Father—explicitly calling the Divine Word (Logos) 'the second God' (deuteros theos), God's 'First-born Son', the 'Name of God', the 'Image of God' through whom the universe was created, and the sinless Cosmic 'High Priest' and 'Advocate' between God and humanity.

Questions and Answers on Genesis.note: Verse-by-verse Jewish commentary on Genesis (Fragment II.62 preserved verbatim in Greek by Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica VII.13), explaining why Genesis 9:6 says 'in the image of God He made man' in the third person.

quotes.quote: (62) Why is it that he speaks as if of some other god, saying that he made man after the image of God, and not that he made him after his own image? (#Ge 9:6). Very appropriately and without any falsehood was this oracular sentence uttered by God, for no mortal thing could have been formed on the similitude of the supreme Father of the universe, but only after the pattern of the second deity, who is the Word of the supreme Being; since it is fitting that the rational soul of man should bear it the type of the divine Word; since in his first Word God is superior to the most rational possible nature.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Writing before the New Testament existed, Philo asks why God speaks in Genesis 9:6 'as if of some other god' ('in the image of God He made man') and answers explicitly that humanity was made in the image of 'the second deity, who is the Word [Logos] of the supreme Being'—distinct from 'the supreme Father of the universe.'

De Agricultura (On Husbandry).note: Exegetical treatise on Genesis 9:20, identifying God's 'First-born Son' and 'Right Word' as the cosmic ruler and the Angel of the Lord in Exodus 23:20.

quotes.quote: For God, like a shepherd and a king, governs (as if they were a flock of sheep) the earth, and the water, and the air, and the fire, and all the plants, and living creatures that are in them, whether mortal or divine; and he regulates the nature of the heaven, and the periodical revolutions of the sun and moon, and the variations and harmonious movements of the other stars, ruling them according to law and justice; appointing, as their immediate superintendent, his own right reason, his first-born son, who is to receive the charge of this sacred company, as the lieutenant of the great king; for it is said somewhere, "Behold, I am he! I will send my messenger before thy face, who shall keep thee in the Road."
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Philo states that God the Great King governs the entire cosmos through 'his own right Word [Logos], his first-born Son,' and explicitly identifies this First-born Son with the divine Messenger/Angel of Exodus 23:20–21 in whom YHWH placed His own Divine Name.

De Confusione Linguarum (On the Confusio.note: Treatise on Genesis 11:1–9 (where God says in the plural, 'Come, let Us go down'), identifying the Divine Word as God's First-born Son, exact Image, and Creator.

quotes.quote: (62) I have also heard of one of the companions of Moses having uttered such a speech as this: "Behold, a man whose name is the East!"{18}{#zec 6:12.} A very novel appellation indeed, if you consider it as spoken of a man who is compounded of body and soul; but if you look upon it as applied to that incorporeal being who in no respect differs from the divine image, you will then agree that the name of the east has been given to him with great felicity. (63) For the Father of the universe has caused him to spring up as the eldest son, whom, in another passage, he calls the firstborn; and he who is thus born, imitating the ways of his father, has formed such and such species, looking to his archetypal patterns.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Expounding the Messianic prophecy of Zechariah 6:12 ('Behold, a man whose name is the Branch/East'), Philo declares that this figure is 'that incorporeal being who in no respect differs from the divine image' (cf. Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15), begotten by 'the Father of the universe' as His 'firstborn Son', who creates all living species by 'imitating the ways of his Father' (compare Jesus' exact words in John 5:19!).

quotes.quote: (146) And even if there be not as yet any one who is worthy to be called a son of God, nevertheless let him labour earnestly to be adorned according to his first-born word, the eldest of his angels, as the great archangel of many names; for he is called, the authority, and the name of God, and the Word, and man according to God's image, and he who sees Israel. (147) For which reason I was induced a little while ago to praise the principles of those who said, "We are all one man's Sons."{43}{#ge 42:11.} For even if we are not yet suitable to be called the sons of God, still we may deserve to be called the children of his eternal image, of his most sacred word; for the image of God is his most ancient word.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Philo lists the Second Temple Jewish titles of this second divine figure: 'His first-born Word', 'the authority [archē / Beginning]', 'the Name of God', 'the Word', 'Man according to God's image', and 'His eternal image'—every one of which the New Testament applies directly to Jesus Christ.

Quis Rerum Divinarum Heres (Who is the H.note: Commentary on God's covenant with Abraham in Genesis 15, describing the Word of God as the personal Mediator and Advocate standing between the Creator and humanity.

quotes.quote: (205) And the Father who created the universe has given to his archangelic and most ancient Word a pre-eminent gift, to stand on the confines of both, and separated that which had been created from the Creator. And this same Word is continually a suppliant to the immortal God on behalf of the mortal race, which is exposed to affliction and misery; and is also the ambassador, sent by the Ruler of all, to the subject race. (206) And the Word rejoices in the gift, and, exulting in it, announces it and boasts of it, saying, "And I stood in the midst, between the Lord and You;"{69}{#nu 16:48.} neither being uncreate as God, nor yet created as you, but being in the midst between these two extremities, like a hostage, as it were, to both parties
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Philo portrays 'the Father' sending His 'most ancient Word' to stand as the personal Mediator and Intercessor between God and humanity, distinguished from all created mortals ('nor yet created as you') and continually interceding before God on behalf of the human race (compare 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1).

De Fuga et Inventione (On Flight and Fin.note: Commentary on Genesis 16:6–14, portraying the Divine Word as the sinless Cosmic High Priest whose Father is God and who speaks from above the Ark of the Covenant.

quotes.quote: (101) But the divine word which is above these does not come into any visible appearance, inasmuch as it is not like to any of the things that come under the external senses, but is itself an image of God, the most ancient of all the objects of intellect in the whole world, and that which is placed in the closest proximity to the only truly existing God, without any partition or distance being interposed between them: for it is said, "I will speak unto thee from above the mercyseat, in the midst, between the two Cherubim."
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Philo identifies the YHWH who spoke to Moses from above the Mercy Seat between the two Cherubim (Exodus 25:22) as the 'Divine Word [Logos]', the 'image of God' who stands in undivided union with the Father ('without any partition or distance being interposed between them').

quotes.quote: For we say that the high priest is not a man, but is the word of God, who has not only no participation in intentional errors, but none even in those which are involuntary. (109) For Moses says that he cannot be defiled neither in respect of his father, that is, the mind, nor his mother, that is, the external sense; {26}{#le 21:11.} because, I imagine, he has received imperishable and wholly pure parents, God being his father, who is also the father of all things, and wisdom being his mother, by means of whom the universe arrived at creation
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Anticipating Hebrews 4:14–15 and 7:26, Philo states that the true heavenly High Priest 'is not a man, but is the Word of God,' utterly sinless ('no participation in intentional errors, nor even in those which are involuntary'), having 'God as his Father.'

De Somniis (On Dreams).note: Two-book treatise on the biblical dreams of Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28 & 31), examining how the God who appeared visibly to Jacob distinguishes Himself from the invisible Father.

quotes.quote: (1.215) For there are, as it seems, two temples belonging to God; one being this world, in which the high priest is the divine word, his own firstborn son. The other is the rational soul, the priest of which is the real true man, the copy of whom, perceptible to the senses, is he who performs his paternal vows and sacrifices, to whom it is enjoined to put on the aforesaid tunic, the representation of the universal heaven, in order that the world may join with the man in offering sacrifice, and that the man may likewise co-operate with the universe.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Decades before the Epistle to the Hebrews was written, a 1st-century Jew identifies the High Priest of the cosmic temple as 'the divine Word [Logos], His [God's] own firstborn Son.'

quotes.quote: (1.228) A very glorious boast for the soul, that God should think fit to appear to and to converse with it. And do not pass by what is here said, but examine it accurately, and see whether there are really two Gods. For it is said: "I am the God who was seen by thee;" not in my place, but in the place of God, as if he meant of some other God. (1.229) What then ought we to say? There is one true God only: but they who are called Gods, by an abuse of language, are numerous; on which account the holy scripture on the present occasion indicates that it is the true God that is meant by the use of the article, the expression being, "I am the God (ho Theos);" but when the word is used incorrectly, it is put without the article, the expression being, "He who was seen by thee in the place," not of the God (tou Theou), but simply "of God" (Theou); (1.230) and what he here calls God is his most ancient word
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Philo examines Genesis 31:13 ('I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God'), asks 'whether there are really two Gods,' and explains that Scripture calls the transcendent Father 'the God' (ho Theos, with the Greek article) and calls His 'most ancient Word [Logos]' who appeared visibly to Jacob 'God' (Theos, without the article)—the exact Greek distinction the Apostle John later used in John 1:1 ('the Word was with ho Theos, and the Word was Theos').

Aramaic Targums (Synagogue Paraphrases o.note: The Aramaic Targums are the ancient liturgical translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible read aloud in Jewish synagogues. Whenever the Hebrew Scriptures describe YHWH appearing visibly on earth, creating humanity, speaking from the burning bush, raining fire on Sodom from YHWH in heaven, or sitting enthroned to hear Israel's prayers, the Targums replace 'the LORD' with 'the Memra (Word) of the Lord'—proving that synagogue Jews already understood 'the Word of the Lord' to be a second, visible Divine Person acting as YHWH on earth long before John wrote 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1).

Targum Onkelos (Babylonian Official Targ.note: The official Aramaic translation of the Torah rooted in 1st-century Judea (attributed in Talmud Megillah 3a to Onkelos under Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua).

quotes.chapter: Genesis 28:20–21 ('The Word of the Lord Will Be My God')
quotes.quote: Yaakov made a vow, saying, If [ the Word of ] Elohim will be with me [ my support ], and guards me on this path that I am going, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear; And if I return in peace to my father's house, and [ the Word of ] Adonoy will be my God;
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: After seeing the Lord standing above the heavenly ladder at Bethel (compare John 1:51), Jacob vows in Targum Onkelos: 'If the Word [Memra] of Elohim will be with me... then the Word [Memra] of the Lord will be my God!'—explicitly worshipping the Word of the Lord as God.

Targum Jonathan on the Prophets.note: The official Aramaic Targum on the Prophets rooted in 1st-century Judea (traditionally linked in the Talmud to Jonathan ben Uzziel, the chief pupil of Hillel the Elder).

quotes.chapter: Isaiah 45:12 ('I Have Made the Earth by My Word')
quotes.quote: It is I who have made the earth by my WORD, and I have created man upon it; it is I who have suspended the heavens by my power, and I have laid the foundation of all the hosts of them.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Where the Hebrew of Isaiah 45:12 says 'I have made the earth, and created man upon it,' Targum Jonathan specifies the divine agent of creation: 'It is I who have made the earth by My WORD [Memra], and I have created man upon it'—providing the direct Jewish foundation for John 1:3 ('All things came into being through Him [the Word]').

quotes.chapter: Isaiah 45:22–25 ('Turn Unto My Word and Be Saved... Every Knee Shall Bow')
quotes.quote: Turn unto my WORD, and be ye saved, all that are at the ends of the earth: for I am the Lord, and there is none else. I have sworn by my WORD, the word is gone forth in righteousness from my presence, and shall not fail, That before me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear. Surely, He has promised to bring me righteousness and strength by the WORD of the Lord. In His WORD they shall offer praise, and all the nations that are incensed against His people shall be ashamed. In the WORD of the Lord all the seed of Israel shall be justified and glorified.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In the very passage that the Apostle Paul applies to Jesus in Philippians 2:10–11 ('that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow'), the 1st-century Aramaic Targum renders God's call as: 'Turn unto My WORD, and be ye saved, all that are at the ends of the earth... In His WORD they shall offer praise... In the WORD of the Lord all the seed of Israel shall be justified and glorified!'

quotes.chapter: Isaiah 48:16 ('Come Near to My Word... The Lord God and His Word Hath Sent Me')
quotes.quote: Come ye near to my WORD; hear ye this; I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; at the time when the nations separated themselves from fearing me, at that time I brought Abraham your father to my service. The prophet saith: And now the Lord God, and His WORD, hath sent me.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 48:16 distinguishes 'the Lord God' and 'His WORD [Memra]' as two coordinated Divine Persons sending the prophet: 'Come ye near to My WORD... And now the Lord God, and His WORD, hath sent me.'

Targum Jerusalem (Palestinian Fragment T.date: c. 2nd–4th Century AD (Preserving Second Temple Liturgical Tradition)
Targum Jerusalem (Palestinian Fragment T.note: Western Palestinian synagogue Targum on the Pentateuch (Targum Yerushalmi II), attributing the creation of man, the 'I AM' of the Burning Bush, and the primordial Light of creation directly to 'the Word (Memra) of the Lord'.

quotes.quote: And the Word of the Lord created man in His likeness, in the likeness of the presence of the Lord He created him, the male and his yoke-fellow He created them.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Where the Hebrew of Genesis 1:27 says 'God created man in His own image,' the Palestinian Targum distinguishes two Divine Persons in creation: 'the Word of the Lord created man in His likeness, in the likeness of the presence of the Lord He created him' (cf. John 1:3; Colossians 1:16).

quotes.chapter: Genesis 3:22 ('Let Us Keep Him from the Garden')
quotes.quote: And the Word of the Lord God said, Behold, Adam whom I have created is sole in my world, as I am sole in the heavens above. It is to be that a great people are to arise from him; from him will arise a people who will know how to discern between good and evil. And now it is good that we keep him from the garden of Eden before he stretch forth his hand and take also of the fruit of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In Genesis 3:22 (where the Hebrew says 'And the LORD God said, Behold, the man has become like one of Us'), the Targum identifies the speaker as 'the Word of the Lord God,' who declares in the first person, 'Adam whom I have created in My world, as I am in the heavens above... let Us keep him from the garden.'

quotes.quote: And the Word of the Lord said to Mosheh, He who spake to the world, Be, and it was; and who will speak to it, Be, and it will be. And he said, Thus shalt thou speak to the sons of Israel, EHEYEH hath sent me unto you.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In the Hebrew text of Exodus 3:14, God speaks from the burning bush and reveals His name 'I AM WHO I AM' (Eheyeh). The Palestinian synagogue Targum explicitly identifies the Divine Person speaking from the bush—who created the universe by His word and whose name is 'I AM' (EHEYEH)—as 'the Word of the Lord' (compare John 8:58!).

quotes.quote: Four nights are there written in the Book of Memorial. Night first; when the Word of the Lord was revealed upon the world as it was created; when the world was without form and void, and darkness was spread upon the face of the deep, and the Word of the Lord illuminated and made it light; and he called it the first night.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Compare this ancient synagogue Passover liturgy directly with John 1:1–5 ('In the beginning was the Word... in Him was life, and the life was the Light of men; and the Light shines in the darkness'): at the creation of the world in Genesis 1:1–3, 'the Word of the Lord was revealed upon the world as it was created... and the Word of the Lord illuminated and made it light.'

Targum Pseudo-Jonathan (Palestinian Targ.date: c. 4th–6th Century AD (Preserving Second Temple & Tannaitic Traditions)
Targum Pseudo-Jonathan (Palestinian Targ.note: Complete Palestinian Aramaic Targum on the Torah depicting the Word (Memra) of the Lord walking in Eden, raining fire from heaven on Sodom, and sitting upon God's high throne hearing Israel's prayers.

quotes.chapter: Genesis 3:8 (The Voice of the Word of the Lord Walking in Eden)
quotes.quote: And they heard the voice of the Word of the Lord God walking in the garden in the repose of the day; and Adam and his wife hid themselves from before the Lord God among the trees of the garden.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: When God walks visibly and audibly in the Garden of Eden in Genesis 3:8, both the Palestinian Targum and the 2nd-century Father Theophilus of Antioch (To Autolycus II.22) identify the Divine Person walking in Paradise as 'the Word of the Lord God.'

quotes.chapter: Genesis 19:24 (Fire Rained Down from Before the Word of the Lord)
quotes.quote: And the Word of the Lord had caused showers of favour to descend upon Sedom and Amorah, to the intent that they might work repentance, but they did it not: so that they said, Wickedness is not manifest before the Lord. Behold, then, there are now sent down upon them sulphur and fire from before the Word of the Lord from Heaven.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Genesis 19:24 ('Then the LORD on earth rained on Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven') was the classic 'Two Powers' text cited by both early Christians (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian) and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 38b). Here the Targum explicitly identifies the YHWH executing judgment on Sodom as 'the Word of the Lord.'

quotes.chapter: Deuteronomy 4:7 (The Word of the Lord Enthroned on High Hearing Prayer)
quotes.quote: For what people so great, to whom the Lord is so nigh in the Name of the Word of the Lord? But the custom of (other) nations is to carry their gods upon their shoulders, that they may seem to be nigh them; but they cannot hear with their ears, (be they nigh or) be they afar off; but the Word of the Lord sitteth upon His throne high and lifted up, and heareth our prayer what time we pray before Him and make our petitions.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In Deuteronomy 4:7 (one of the plural 'Two Powers' verses debated in Talmud Sanhedrin 38b), the Targum declares that the Lord is near to Israel 'in the Name of the Word of the Lord,' and that 'the Word of the Lord sits upon His throne high and lifted up (cf. Isaiah 6:1; John 12:41) and hears our prayer when we pray before Him!'

Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael (Early Tannait.note: The Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael is the earliest halakhic and aggadic rabbinic commentary on the Book of Exodus (compiled from 2nd-century AD Tannaitic traditions). In commenting on Exodus 15:3 and Exodus 20:2, it explicitly addresses the 'Two Powers in Heaven' controversy—recording how early Jewish believers argued for 'two Deities' because Scripture depicts YHWH appearing visibly in two distinct forms: as a young warrior at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:3) and as the white-haired Ancient of Days enthroned in Daniel 7:9–10.

Tractate Bahodesh & Tractate Shirata.note: Early Tannaitic polemic against Jewish believers who argued for 'Two Deities' from the visible manifestations of YHWH in Exodus 15:3, Exodus 24:10, and Daniel 7:9–10.

quotes.chapter: Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 20:2:2 ('Those Heretics Who Contend That There Are Two Deities')
quotes.quote: "I am the L–rd your G–d who took you out of the land of Egypt." What is the intent of this? Because He appeared at the Red Sea as a hero waging war, viz. (Exodus 15:3) "The L–rd is a Man of war," and at Mount Sinai, as an elder full of mercy, so as not to provide an opening for the nations of the world to say that there are two Deities, (He said) "I am the L–rd your G–d." ... R. Nathan says: This is the retort to those heretics who would contend that there are two Deities.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Look at Rabbi Nathan's admission: 2nd-century Jewish 'heretics' (Minim) pointed to the fact that God appeared visibly as 'a Man of war' at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:3) and as the Ancient of Days at Sinai/Daniel 7:9 to contend that there are two Divine Persons ('two Deities') within the God of Israel!

Babylonian Talmud (Talmud Bavli).note: After the rise of Christianity in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, rabbinic authorities sought to suppress the older Second Temple Jewish belief in 'Two Powers in Heaven' (Hebrew: Shtei Reshuyot ba-Shamayim), branding it a heresy (minut). Yet in recording their debates against Jewish-Christian and binitarian 'heretics' (Minim), the Babylonian Talmud inadvertently preserved proof that even the greatest early rabbis (like Rabbi Akiva in AD 120) taught two thrones in heaven—one for God and one for the Messiah—and admitted that the Hebrew Scriptures speak of a second 'Lord' who bears God's own Name.

Tractate Hagigah (Folios 14a & 15a).note: Contains the two most famous 'Two Powers in Heaven' passages in rabbinic literature: Rabbi Akiva's teaching that the second heavenly throne of Daniel 7:9 is for the Messiah (14a), and Elisha ben Abuyah's cry upon seeing a second seated Ruler in heaven: 'Perhaps there are Two Powers in Heaven!' (15a).

quotes.chapter: Hagigah 14a (Rabbi Akiva's Two Thrones in Heaven: 'One for God and One for David')
quotes.quote: One throne is for Him and one is for David, as it is taught in a baraita with regard to this issue: One throne for Him and one for David; this is the statement of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili said to him: Akiva, how long shall you make the Divine Presence profane, by presenting it as though one could sit next to Him? Rather, the two thrones are designated for different purposes: One for judgment and one for righteousness.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In Daniel 7:9, Daniel sees plural 'thrones' set up in heaven ('till thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days did sit'). Rabbi Akiva (c. AD 50–135), the most revered sage of rabbinic Judaism, preserved the older Jewish teaching that the two heavenly thrones are 'one throne for Him [God] and one for David [the Messiah]'—until his alarmed colleague Rabbi Yosei rebuked him for placing the Messiah on a heavenly throne beside God!

quotes.chapter: Hagigah 15a ('Perhaps There Are Two Authorities [Two Powers] in Heaven!')
quotes.quote: The Gemara poses a question: What was it that led him to heresy? He saw the angel Mitatron, who was granted permission to sit and write the merits of Israel. He said: There is a tradition that in the world above there is no sitting; no competition; no turning one’s back before Him, i.e., all face the Divine Presence; and no lethargy. Seeing that someone other than God was seated above, he said: Perhaps, the Gemara here interjects, Heaven forbid, there are two authorities, and there is another source of power in control of the world in addition to God. Such thoughts led Aḥer to heresy.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: This is the passage that gave the 'Two Powers in Heaven' (shtei reshuyot) doctrine its name. In Jewish tradition, no angel or creature is ever permitted to sit in heaven ('in the world above there is no sitting'). When the 2nd-century rabbi Elisha ben Abuyah (Aḥer) saw a second figure seated upon a throne in heaven, he immediately concluded: 'Perhaps there are Two Powers [two divine authorities] in heaven!'—the exact claim Jesus made before the Sanhedrin when He declared that they would see the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power' (Mark 14:62).

Tractate Megillah (Folio 9a).date: c. AD 500 (Preserving Tannaitic Baraita on the Septuagint)
Tractate Megillah (Folio 9a).note: Records the early Tannaitic account of why the 72 Jewish elders translating the Torah into Greek altered the plural verses of Genesis so readers would not conclude there are 'Two Powers'.

quotes.chapter: Megillah 9a (Altering 'Let Us Make Man' So Readers Would Not See 'Two Powers')
quotes.quote: And they wrote for him: God created in the beginning [bereshit], reversing the order of the words in the first phrase in the Torah that could be misinterpreted as: “Bereshit created God” (Genesis 1:1). They did so to negate those who believe in the preexistence of the world and those who maintain that there are two powers in the world: One is Bereshit, who created the second, God. And they wrote: I shall make man in image and in likeness, rather than: “Let us make man in our image and in our likeness” (Genesis 1:26), as from there too one could mistakenly conclude that there are multiple powers and that God has human form.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: The Talmud claims that when the 72 elders translated the Torah for King Ptolemy, they felt compelled to change 'Let Us make man in Our image' (Genesis 1:26) to the singular 'I shall make man' specifically to stop readers from concluding 'that there are two powers in the world' and 'that there are multiple powers and that God has human form'!

Tractate Sanhedrin (Folios 38b & 98a).note: Records the rabbinic debates against Jewish 'Two Powers' believers (Minim) over Genesis 1:26, Genesis 11:7, Genesis 19:24, Exodus 24:1, Exodus 23:20–21, and Daniel 7:9–14.

quotes.chapter: Sanhedrin 38b (Torah Verses Cited by Jewish 'Two Powers' Believers)
quotes.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: Any place in the Bible from where the heretics attempt to prove their heresy, i.e., that there is more than one god, the response to their claim is alongside them, i.e., in the immediate vicinity of the verses they cite. The verse states that God said: “Let us make man in our image” (Genesis 1:26), employing the plural, but it then states: “And God created man in His image” (Genesis 1:27), employing the singular. The verse states that God said: “Come, let us go down and there confound their language” (Genesis 11:7), but it also states: “And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower” (Genesis 11:5). The verse states in the plural: “There God was revealed [niglu] to him when he fled from the face of his brother” (Genesis 35:7)
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Rabbi Yoḥanan openly admits that Jewish 'heretics' (Minim) proved a plurality of Persons within the one Godhead directly from the Hebrew grammar of the Torah: plural divine speech in Genesis 1:26 ('Let Us make man in Our image') and Genesis 11:7 ('Come, let Us go down'), and plural verbs combined with singular verbs—which Christians pointed out reflects multiple Persons (plural) sharing one divine essence (singular)!

quotes.chapter: Sanhedrin 38b (The Second 'Lord' of Exodus 24:1 Who Bears God's Own Name)
quotes.quote: The Gemara relates: A certain heretic said to Rav Idit: It is written in the verse concerning God: “And to Moses He said: Come up to the Lord” (Exodus 24:1). The heretic raised a question: It should have stated: Come up to Me. Rav Idit said to him: This term, “the Lord,” in that verse is referring to the angel Metatron, whose name is like the name of his Master, as it is written: “Behold I send an angel before you to keep you in the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Take heed of him and obey his voice; do not defy him; for he will not pardon your transgression, for My name is in him” (Exodus 23:20–21). The heretic said to him: If so, if this angel is equated with God, we should worship him
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: Look at this remarkable exchange: a Jewish 'heretic' (a Jewish-Christian or 'Two Powers' believer) points out that in Exodus 24:1, God speaks of a second 'Lord' ('And to Moses He said: Come up to the Lord'—instead of 'Come up to Me'). Rav Idit is forced to admit that 'the Lord' in Exodus 24:1 is the divine Mediator of Exodus 23:20–21 'whose name is like the name of his Master' ('for My Name [YHWH] is in him')—prompting the challenger to reply: 'If so, if this figure is equated with God, we should worship him as we worship God!'

quotes.chapter: Sanhedrin 38b (The Two 'Lords' of Genesis 19:24: One on Earth, One in Heaven)
quotes.quote: The Gemara relates: A certain heretic said to Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei: It is written: “And the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (Genesis 19:24). The heretic raised the question: It should have stated: From Him out of heaven.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In Genesis 19:24, the LORD (who had just spoken visibly with Abraham on earth in Genesis 18) rains fire on Sodom 'from the LORD out of heaven.' This Talmudic passage proves that ancient Jewish believers pointed to Genesis 19:24—the exact same verse used by 2nd-century Christians Justin Martyr and Irenaeus—to show two Divine Persons sharing the name YHWH: the Lord on earth and the Lord in heaven.

quotes.quote: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi raises a contradiction between two depictions of the coming of the Messiah. It is written: “There came with the clouds of heaven, one like unto a son of man… and there was given him dominion and glory and a kingdom…his dominion is an everlasting dominion” (Daniel 7:13–14). And it is written: “Behold, your king will come to you; he is just and victorious; lowly and riding upon a donkey and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Rabbi Alexandri explains: If the Jewish people merit redemption, the Messiah will come in a miraculous manner with the clouds of heaven. If they do not merit redemption, the Messiah will come lowly and riding upon a donkey.
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In the Hebrew Bible, riding upon the clouds of heaven belongs exclusively to YHWH alone (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1). Yet here the Talmud confirms that the 'One like a Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven' in Daniel 7:13—whom Jesus identified as Himself at His trial in Mark 14:62, causing the High Priest to tear his robes—is indeed the divine King-Messiah.

Tractate Sukkah (Folio 52a).note: Preserves the early rabbinic interpretation applying Zechariah 12:10 ('they shall look unto Me whom they have pierced') to the slain Messiah.

quotes.chapter: Sukkah 52a ('They Shall Look Unto Me Whom They Have Pierced' Applied to the Messiah)
quotes.quote: Apropos the eulogy at the end of days, the Gemara asks: For what is the nature of this eulogy? The Gemara answers: Rabbi Dosa and the Rabbis disagree concerning this matter. One said that this eulogy is for Messiah ben Yosef who was killed in the war of Gog from the land of Magog prior to the ultimate redemption with the coming of Messiah ben David. And one said that this eulogy is for the evil inclination that was killed. The Gemara asks: Granted, according to the one who said that the lament is for Messiah ben Yosef who was killed, this would be the meaning of that which is written in that context: “And they shall look unto Me because they have thrust him through; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son” (Zechariah 12:10).
quotes.note: Two Powers in Heaven: In Zechariah 12:1, 10, the speaker is YHWH Himself, who stretches out the heavens and says: 'And they shall look unto Me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son.' Here the Talmud admits that Zechariah 12:10 refers to the piercing and death of the Messiah—confirming John 19:37!
